title: The expense of spirit
short: The spending of vital energy and semen; Renaissance physiology held that sex consumed the body's 'spirits' and shortened life.
body: 'Expense' means expenditure, outlay (OED); 'spirit' means the vital spirits, the vital force of body and mind, and also semen, a sense editors (Booth, Kerrigan, Duncan-Jones) all note. The common belief that each sexual act cost a man some of his life underlies the phrase. The Quarto prints 'Th' expence', making the line regular; the archive text spells out 'The expense', so the first foot must be read with elision. The line is impersonal: unlike most sonnets in the sequence, 129 has no 'I' and no 'you', as Vendler notes, and speaks as general moral analysis.

title: a waste of shame
short: In a shameful squandering; 'waste' also suggests a barren wasteland, and many critics hear a pun on 'waist'.
body: The phrase works several ways at once: the spending happens in shameful waste; it takes place in a desert ('waste') of shame; and, with Elizabethan spelling and pronunciation, 'waste' could pun on 'waist', the body (Booth, Duncan-Jones). 'Shame' may also refer to the genitals, as in the Latin pudenda. Booth gives the fullest account of the layered meanings and argues that the line's density is the point.

title: Is lust in action: and till action, lust
short: Lust in action (the sexual act) is a shameful expenditure; and before it is acted, lust is all the vices listed next.
body: The sentence first defines lust as consummated act, then turns ('and till action') to lust before consummation. The chiasmus (lust in action / till action, lust) traps the reader between the two states. The sonnet's structure follows the stages of desire: before, during and after. 'In action' may also carry a theatrical or legal sense (an action at law), which some readers connect with 'perjur'd'.

anchor: perjur'd, murderous, bloody, full of blame
title: perjur'd, murderous, bloody ... (asyndeton)
short: A breathless string of adjectives without conjunctions (asyndeton) piles up the vices of lust before it is satisfied.
body: The list runs over two lines and nine descriptive terms with no 'and', the rhetorical figure asyndeton, which conveys compulsive, uncontrolled energy. 'Perjur'd' because lust breaks vows and swears false oaths; 'bloody' and 'murderous' because it can lead to violence, as in Lucrece; 'rude' = brutal, violent; 'not to trust' = untrustworthy. Vendler and Booth both treat the cramming of the quatrain as an enactment of frenzy. Riding and Graves print the Quarto's spellings ('periurd', 'murdrous', 'blouddy') and discuss their pronunciation.

anchor: Enjoy'd no sooner but despised straight
title: Enjoy'd no sooner but despised straight
short: As soon as lust is satisfied it is at once despised.
body: 'Straight' means immediately, straightaway. The line states the classic post-coital disgust found in moral and medical writing since antiquity; editors compare Lucrece (from l. 690), where Tarquin's lust turns to loathing after the rape. The rapid 'no sooner ... but' construction is repeated in l. 6, setting up the parallel lines of hunting and hating. The speed of the verse mimics the speed of the change from appetite to disgust.

title: Past reason hunted ... Past reason hated
short: Lust is pursued beyond all reason, and once possessed, hated beyond reason; the repeated phrase (anaphora) makes the two extremes mirror each other.
body: 'Past reason' means beyond the control of reason, the faculty that should govern appetite in Renaissance moral psychology. The repetition at the start of l. 6 and l. 7 (anaphora) shows that desire and loathing are equally irrational. 'Hunted' leads into the bait and trap imagery that follows. Booth notes the way the verbs slide from the lustful person to lust itself as their subject.

title: a swallow'd bait ... to make the taker mad
short: Lust is like poisoned bait deliberately set to drive whoever swallows it mad.
body: The image is of a hunting or fishing bait laced with poison, laid 'on purpose' to madden the creature that takes it. 'Taker' is the one who takes the bait (and, sexually, who takes the partner). The idea of a trap laid on purpose suggests a deliberate snare, perhaps by the woman, or by nature, or by the devil; critics differ on who lays it. The word 'mad' is then picked up at once in l. 9, linking quatrains.

title: Mad in pursuit (Quarto 'Made In pursut')
short: Editors emend the Quarto's 'Made In pursut' to 'Mad in pursuit', linking back to 'mad' in l. 8; some critics defend the Quarto reading.
body: The 1609 Quarto reads 'Made In pursut', which most editors since the eighteenth century print as 'Mad in pursuit', taking 'Made' as a spelling or compositor's error. Riding and Graves (1927) argued that the original spelling and punctuation keep a richer sense, and that modern editing flattens the poem. Booth discusses the case and keeps 'Mad' while acknowledging the interplay. The line says lust is mad both while pursuing and while possessing ('in possession so').

title: Had, having, and in quest, to have
short: Extreme in all tenses of desire: when it has had, while it is having, and while still seeking to have.
body: The line runs through the verb 'have' in three forms (polyptoton): past ('Had'), present ('having') and future or desired ('in quest, to have'). It summarizes the whole sonnet's analysis of before, during and after. 'Extreme' applies to every stage. Riding and Graves argue that the Quarto's lighter punctuation lets the line connect with the previous and next lines rather than standing alone. The verb 'have' also had sexual force.

anchor: A bliss in proof, and proved
title: A bliss in proof, and proved, a very woe
short: A delight while being experienced, and once experienced, a real misery; the Quarto reads 'and proud and very wo', which some prefer.
body: 'In proof' means in the experience, while being tried; 'proved' means once tried, afterwards; 'very' means true, real. The Quarto prints 'A blisse in proofe and proud and very wo'. Most editors emend 'proud' to 'prov'd' and add commas, so that bliss comes during and woe after. Riding and Graves argued that the Quarto's version makes lust a bliss and a woe at every stage, and that modern punctuation reduces it to a simple sequence. Booth weighs both and notes that 'proud' could also suggest sexual swelling. The disagreement remains a classic crux.

anchor: a joy propos'd; behind a dream
title: a joy propos'd; behind a dream
short: Before the act, a joy one looks forward to; after it, only an illusion that has vanished.
body: 'Propos'd' means set before one as an aim, anticipated. 'Behind' means afterwards, looking back. The 'dream' is the empty memory of a pleasure that seems unreal once over. The line completes the time-sequence of the sonnet in compact antithesis. Editors compare the dream language of Lucrece, ll. 211-12, where lustful pleasure is called 'a dream, a breath, a froth of fleeting joy'.

anchor: well knows; yet none knows well
title: the world well knows; yet none knows well
short: Everyone knows all this; yet no one knows how to act on the knowledge; a chiasmus (well knows / knows well).
body: The reversal of 'well knows' and 'knows well' (chiasmus, or antimetabole) moves from mere knowledge to practical wisdom: knowing a fact versus knowing how to live by it. The couplet acknowledges the Ovidian and Pauline truth that knowledge of the good does not stop us doing evil (compare Romans 7:19: 'the good that I would I do not'). Vendler highlights the couplet's turn from analysis to the admission of helplessness.

title: the heaven ... this hell
short: The heaven of sexual bliss that leads to the hell of shame and damnation; 'hell' was also slang for the female sexual organs.
body: The religious antithesis of heaven and hell is literal (the soul's damnation for sin) and psychological (bliss turning to torment). Booth and Duncan-Jones note that 'hell' was Elizabethan slang for the vagina, a sense used in Sonnet 144 ('I guess one angel in another's hell'). The line therefore ends in a pun that is both disgusted and theological. Critics disagree on how misogynistic the poem is: some read the trap as laid by the woman, others by human nature itself.
